name: Abimael
title: Descendant of Shem through Joktan
lifespan: Unknown; likely late 3rd or early 2nd millennium BC
summary: Abimael belongs to Joktan's lineage and is counted among his thirteen sons, listed in the table of nations after the flood. Through Joktan and Eber, he descends from Shem, Noah's eldest son. His name carries a theophoric meaning – 'my father is God' – and testifies to divine awareness in early naming traditions. The Joktanites are traditionally linked to the Arabian Peninsula, and Abimael's place in the genealogy points to his role as ancestor of one of the peoples who spread after the Babel event. Both Genesis and 1 Chronicles preserve his name in the line from Shem.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy after Shem
keyEvents.description: Abimael is listed as one of the thirteen sons of Joktan in the genealogy following Noah's son Shem. This genealogy shows the spread of nations after the flood.

keyEvents.title: The Sons of Joktan and Their Settlement Area
keyEvents.description: Joktan's sons, including Abimael, settled in the mountainous region to the east, between Mesha and Sephar. This indicates a connection to the southern Arabian Peninsula.

keyEvents.title: Origins of Nations from Shem's Lineage
keyEvents.description: Abimael is mentioned as part of Shem's lineage, which formed an important part of the nations that spread across the earth after the flood.

keyEvents.title: Repetition in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Abimael's place in family history is confirmed in 1 Chronicles, where the genealogy from Adam to the tribes of Israel is given. He is mentioned again as a son of Joktan.

keyEvents.title: Eber's Two Sons and the Division of Peoples
keyEvents.description: Abimael's grandfather Eber had two sons: Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided, and Joktan, who became the father of Abimael and his brothers. This division marks an important point in biblical history.

versions.summary: Abimael was a son of Joktan and a descendant of Shem, Noah's son. He is mentioned in the Bible's genealogies as one of the many sons of Joktan and is regarded as the ancestor of an Arab people. His name may mean 'my father is God' or 'God is my father'.
versions.title: Descendant of Shem
versions.reason: [minor] According to Gen 10:26-29, Joktan had thirteen sons, but the description says "thirteen". Let us verify: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, Jobab = 13 sons. This is correct, but the list of siblings in family contains only 12 (Abimael himself is not included, which is standard practice). The description is therefore accurate.; [minor] Gen 10:29 mentions Abimael directly, while verse 30 concerns the settlement area. Abimael is actually mentioned in verse 28 (according to some translations) or verses 28-29 (depending on the division). Verse 29 is correct for Abimael in many translations, but it should be checked that verse 28 has already been covered in the first instance.; [minor] The phrasing "Bible's genealogies" can be simplified to "the genealogies in Genesis". Furthermore, the summary could be enriched with a bit more contextual information about Joktan's line and its significance for the table of nations.; [minor] The role "patriarch" is acceptable, but "ancestor" might be more precise since Abimael is primarily known as an ancestor of a people rather than a patriarch in the traditional biblical sense (like Abraham, Isaac, Jacob).; [minor] The dating "c. 2000 BC" is very approximate. Joktan's generation is traditionally placed closer to c. 2200–2100 BC in biblical chronology, depending on the calculation method. A broader formulation such as "Unknown; probably early 2nd millennium BC" may be more precise.

versions.summary: Abimael was a son of Joktan and a descendant of Shem, Noah's son. He is mentioned in the genealogies in Genesis and 1 Chronicles as one of the thirteen sons of Joktan and is regarded as the ancestor of an Arab people. Joktan's descendants are traditionally linked to the southern Arabian Peninsula. The name Abimael is usually interpreted as 'my father is God' or 'God is my father', reflecting a theophory—a divine reference in a personal name.
versions.title: Descendant of Shem through Joktan
versions.reason: [minor] Gen 10:29 mentions several of Joktan's sons (including Abimael), but verse 30 concerns the area of settlement. It is correct to include both verses in this event, which deals with the area of settlement, but Abimael is actually mentioned in verse 28, not verse 29. Verse 29 lists other sons. Nevertheless, the event primarily concerns the area of settlement (verse 30), so the connection is acceptable.; [minor] The summary is well phrased, but it resembles version 1 structurally ('Abimael was a son of Joktan and a descendant of Shem, Noah's son. He is mentioned in the genealogies...'). It should be rephrased to distinguish itself more clearly from earlier versions.; [minor] The dating 'probably early 2nd millennium BC' is uncertain. footnotes.text: The name Abimael (Hebrew: אֲבִימָאֵל) is composed of 'avi' (my father) and 'El' (God), and is commonly interpreted as 'my father is God' or 'God is my father'. This type of theophoric name—names containing a divine reference—was widespread among Semitic peoples and testifies to an awareness of the divine in naming traditions.

Joktan and his sons, including Abimael, are traditionally linked to South Arabia. In Arab genealogies, Joktan (Arabic: Qaḥṭān) is identified as the ancestor of the southern Arabian tribes. Several of Joktan's sons' names have been attempted to be connected with known place names or tribal names on the Arabian Peninsula, strengthening the connection between the table of nations and historical geography.

The table of nations in Genesis 10 is a unique document from the ancient world, providing a systematic overview of the origins and spread of peoples after the flood. The settlement area of the Joktanites is described as extending 'from Mesha to Sephar, the mountain region in the east' (Gen 10:30), and this has been attempted to be identified with various regions in the southern Arabian highlands, including Yemen and Oman.

In rabbinic tradition, Joktan's lineage has received less attention than Peleg's line, since it is through Peleg that the connection to Abraham and the people of Israel continues. The names in Joktan's line are nevertheless preserved as a witness that Noah's descendants spread out and filled the earth, in accordance with God's command after the flood.

The division that took place 'in the days of Peleg' (Gen 10:25) has been interpreted in various ways: as a reference to the confusion of languages at Babel (Gen 11), as a geographical or political division of peoples, or as a combination of these. This division forms the historical context for the spread of Joktan's sons, including Abimael, to their respective settlement areas.
